name: Pearl Gentian
lede: Pearl Gentian is a dark, greenish teal from the German RAL paint standard, named for a flower it is nothing like in color.

sections.title: Pearl, not petrol
sections.body:
Our library catalogues this color from RAL 5025, issued under the RAL industrial color standard first published in Germany in 1927 [1]. The gentian flower it borrows from blooms a bright, saturated blue; this swatch is darker, greyer and pulled toward green, closer to the ISCC-NBS block "moderate greenish blue" than to any flower petal [1]. In Munsell it sits at 6.1B 3.9/4.7, and it shares the small "Pearl" naming family with [[heather-grey|Pearl Blackberry]] and [[spruce-green|Pearl Green]], three unconnected hues joined only by that borrowed gem-word [1].

The nearest named colors in our data are [[dark-peacock|Bluish petrol]] and [[dark-peacock|Dark peacock]], both 2.6 CIEDE2000 units away — near enough that either could stand in for Pearl Gentian on screen [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Pearl Gentian appears in 120 of our 23,781 paintings, about 0.5 percent, as photographed; the within-painting lens finds it in 53 of them [2]. It peaks in the 1900s, at 2.3 times the expected rate for that century [2]. Inside a painting it most often plays a hidden color, present but not carrying the light [2].

The earliest match is dated 1433, in a work by Robert Campin — 494 years before RAL's 1927 record of the name, as photographed, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [2]. The gap is a look-alike hue surviving in an aged photograph, not evidence of the paint itself that early [2].

questions.q: Gentian flowers are usually a bright, saturated blue. How does Pearl Gentian the color compare?
True or false: Pearl Gentian most often appears as a painting's brightest highlight in our archive.

openers: Pearl Gentian is named for a flower far brighter and bluer than the color itself.
